ghaṭasphoṭa
(‘[the rite of] breaking a pot’)
------------------------------------------
Though it is human to err and divine to forgive, there are human beings addicted to committing heinous sins but reluctant to repent or perform expiations. घट-sphoṭa is the ritual method of excommunicating such incorrigibles from the society.
In this rite, a घट or an earthen pot, filled with dirty water is kept on a bed of दर्भ grass and a slave girl or man is made to kick it with her or his left foot so that it is overturned, spilling all the water. By this ritual, the sinner is considered to have become dead for the society. His near relatives observe—after this ghaṭasphoṭa—aśauca (ceremonial impurity) and also offer piṇḍas (rice-balls) in his name as to a dead person.

Ghaṭotkaca
(‘one [whose head] is hairless [like that of] a घट or pot’)
------------------------------------------
Out of the many characters of the Mahābhārata, that of घटोत्कच is rather short, but interesting. Born absolutely bald, without any hair on his head (hence the name घट + ut + कच = घटोत्कच). He was the son of भीम (the second of the Pāṇḍava heroes) and Hiḍimbā, the sister of the demon Hiḍimbāsura whom भीम had slain. As per the boon received by the rākṣasa (or demon) race from the goddess पार्वती, any offspring of the राक्षसस् would attain adulthood immediately after birth itself. So घटोत्कच attained physical and mental adulthood soon after birth. When भीम left Hiḍimbā and her son घटोत्कच to rejoin his brothers and मोथेर्, घटोत्कच promised to help him and serve him in any way, as soon as he just remembered this son of his.
He helped the Pāṇḍavas in several ways especially when they were under-going banishment in the forest.
He fought the Kauravas fiercely on behalf of the Pāṇḍavas but was killed by कर्ण who was forced to use his weapon शक्ति, which he had reserved for अर्जुन!

ghaṭam
------------------------------------------
Indian मुसिच्, though originally one, gradually branched off into two systems: the North Indian (Uttarādi) and the South Indian (Dakṣiṇādi). The South Indian classical मुसिच् retained its original flavour whereas the North Indian system attained a distinctness of its own due to the Persian influence wrought during the Mughal period.
Among the percussion instruments used in the South Indian classical music—vocal or instrumental—the mṛdaṅgam is the most important. The next in importance is the घटम्. It is actually a large earthen pot carefully prepared so as to give a musical sound when beaten, with the finger-tips and palms of the hands.
Unlike the mṛdaṅgam, the śruti or the tonic of the घटम् cannot be changed. Hence, the player of a घटम् generally keeps a large number of them to suit the different śrutis of the singers.

ghaṭa
(‘a pot’)
------------------------------------------
A घट or a mud-pot is an important accessory in many a Hindu ritual. When filled with water and decorated with certain leaves and coconut it becomes fit for any deity being ceremonially invoked into it. Such a घट is also called a kumbha or a कलश. It is one of the four receptacles of divinity, the other three being अग्नि (fire), vigraha (icon) and स्थण्डिल (consecrated platform).
It is sometimes used as an art motif indicating auspiciousness and abundance, on the pillars and doors in temples.
A ceremonially installed pot is an essential part of the worship of the Divine मोथेर् दुर्गा during the नवरात्र festival.
According to the works on हठयोग, घट or ghaṭāvasthā is a state of prāṇā-yāma. In this state, the two prāṇas or vital airs—the प्राण and the apāna—are in a balanced state leading to the union of the जीव (individual सोउल्) with परमात्मन् (the Supreme सोउल्).
In philosophical and mystical treatises, the word ‘ghaṭa’ is sometimes used to indicate the body, since it is as fragile as a mudpot.
